body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: On Wednesday was first performed a musical drama in three acts, called Kamtchatka, or the Slaves’ Tribute, being an adaptation of Mr. Kotzebue’s play of Count Benyowski, by Mr. Charles Kemble. We had fondly hoped that we should hear no more of the German drama, till at least it should wear the charm of novelty again with an English audience; but Mr. Charles Kemble has the misfortune to have a taste for the literature of that country, and the good luck to command the ear of the Managers. The new drama promised shew, procession and music; with these alliances, the new theatre can now command the town; and, notwithstanding the just dissatisfaction and disgust with which Kamtchatka was received on its first night, we dare say we shall not hear of its last night for some time to come. We take the following Dramatis Personae from the Song-books which are sold in the House:

body.p: The drama of Kamtchatka is little other than an abridgment of Kotzebue’s play; but Mr. Charles Kemble is at least answerable for its adoption; and he could scarcely have attempted to naturalize in England a play which would be more alien to our feelings. Count Benyowski was a Hungarian, who took part in one of the Polish confederacies, with which the Russians waged war with their usual success. The drama opens with the arrival of the captive Benyowski as a Russian exile to Kamtchatka, where he is immediately introduced to the Governor’s house, and complimented upon his services in navigating the ship in which he arrived, upon some casualty, we believe, which befel its captain. The governor’s daughter, who had long wanted something to do, falls in love with him on the instant, and immediately proposes to her father that the exile should be engaged to teach her French; the Governor consents; and the first lesson is actually given on the stage, during which, the pupil addresses a good deal of silly German love to her master, from whom she requires only the French for The heart beats,—Le Cœur palpite,—of which she makes as much as Monsieur Jourdain does of his Belle marquise. But Benyowski is a conspirator, as well as a French-master; and is elected (not without opposition) chief of a band of his fellow-exiles, who are conspiring to escape. The opposition-candidate for the same honour is Stepanof, jealous of the Count both as a lover and as a warrior. This truly Russian character is as vehement against a foreigner and a Hungarian captain, as any truly British reformist; and stands a poll against him; but the Count carries his election hollow. Benyowski thus plays two games; for the Governor, in the mean time, at the importunity of his daughter, offers him that young lady in marriage, and his liberty besides, neither of which does Benyowski refuse. Stepanof accuses him of this duplicity, but he is acquitted of it by his Peers; and, we believe, it is for an attempt to murder his leader that Stepanof himself is condemned by the same Jury. But, new wonders! Benyowski, the injured party, pardons his rival; and to convince him that he cannot marry the Governor's daughter, shews him the picture of his own wife, and informs him that he is also a father. Stepanof appears satisfied; and, upon the same disclosure being at length made to Athanasia herself, who arrives to assist the conspiracy, ventures to prefer his suit. The unhappy Athanasia professes not the less love for the Count because he is a husband and a father; talks of following him all the world over, and rejects Stepanof with horror. The disappointed man grows furious; discloses the conspiracy to the Governor; refuses his freedom for this service; returns to Benyowski; triumphs when his treachery is discovered; and stabs himself in the frenzied exultation. But the exile conspirators are reinforced; the game's afoot; the Governor’s castle is possessed; and he himself dragged in chains to the shore, whence the exiles embark for freedom. He is here set at liberty, and his daughter is refused by the ungrateful Benyowski the pleasure of accompanying him; the Governor bestows a curse upon her as horrible as King Lear’s upon Goneril; and the curtain falls.

This story is a perfect instance of the German passion for something violent and striking: their dramatists shock the feelings, instead of interesting them. All this disproportion of cause and effect, this gratuitous agitation of the mind, does not suit the meridian of English taste, which revolts from such a hero as Benyowski, instead of suffering itself to be borne along with his fortunes and his fate. An English hero must not serve two masters; he must not conspire against the Governor with his brothers in exile, at the same time that he is performing the part of bridegroom to the Governor’s own daughter, and partaking of his festival hospitality. This German drama does not contain a single character that tells with our audience; and we are not very fearful of its becoming a favourite with them.

The comic characters, with which it is attempted to lighten the piece, are very dull and very vulgar, and manifest that Mr. C. Kemble has no vein for the humorous. Even Mr. Liston failed to elicit a laugh. The serious songs are written with more of that gentlemanly spirit, which we should take their author to possess, and are entitled to praise, in these days, when it is indifferent in point of taste, whether you buy your song-book from off a wall in Wapping, or from one of the fruiteresses of our theatres. The general music of this drama is the composition of Mr. Welsh, and the overture is by Mr. Ware. The theatre may find these gentlemen very useful composers, always at hand, and open to direction; but the musical genius of England will not be much encouraged by employing them upon great occasions. Mr. Sinclair’s second melody was pleasing, and was warbled most delightfully; but Mr. Welsh should have better known the powers of his pupil (as we understand Mr. Sinclar to be) than to task him to a bravura so greatly beyond his strength as the third song. We are happy, for the cause of good music, to find that it is not in the wonderful, the surprising, the rapid transition, the tour de voix, that Mr. Sinclair's talents lie; it is in the melodious, the pleasing, the touching, the tender.

Scarcely was the pen dry, with which we wrote our observations on the practice of drawing characters at and for particular actors, when a musical afterpiece, called the Green-ey'd Monster, or How to get your Money, was produced by Mr. Pocock, the leading character of which was written expressly for Mr. Mathews, was by him rehearsed last season, and is now, by reason of his non-engagement, thrust upon the shoulders of poor Mr. Lovegrove. We really witnessed this gentleman's execution of his trust, with as much pain as it was evident he felt in the performance of it. It was a character, the very gist of which was to deceive by personation, and by rapid succession of disguise and mimicry. Now, Mr. Mathews has the most flexible countenance and voice in the world; not his voice alone, but his face and mind readily transform themselves into those of any man of peculiarities, and he does not so much imitate this or that character, as become this or that character, by a kind of temporary metempsychosis. Of other mimics, you say, "shut your eyes, and you may fancy the man is present." Of Mr. Mathews it may be said, "open your eyes, and you will see the man, as well as hear him." That actor's stage-mimicries really deceive half the audience, who count as many different men as he personates characters in the same piece; and we are sure that many a simple gallery spectator has positively gone away from the theatre with the mistake unrectified. Now Mr. Lovegrove has one of the hardest faces on the stage, unchangeable as a hatchet, to which Mr. Dowton, with much truth, jestingly compares it. Mr. Lovegrove puts on several disguises in the Farce before us; but
"Look in his face and you'll forget them all." Through every one of them may be seen, not the cloven foot, but the cleaving head, the aforesaid hatchet face. Two or three of these personations were of the parts of creditors, where a long face is somewhat in character; but how did the round bellied inn-keeper, who was one of those creditors, come honestly by such a thing? That Mr. Lovegrove has no mimic vein at all, we are not prepared to say; but we do not think that mine will repay the digging, and we are sure he has better talents. To engage a man to play Lord Ogleby, and other parts of high comedy, so meritoriously, and then to precipitate him into Mr. Pocock's low farces!

The scenic arrangement of the Green-ey’d Monster is just one degree above that of a judicious and well-bred Harlequinade. It has the same number of face-slamming doors, down-tumbling tables, and out-jumping windows. After the manner of Miss Baillie's series of Plays on the Passions, the Green-ey’d Monster is intended to illustrate the passion of Jealousy. An old husband is jealous of a young wife; a young wife is jealous of an old husband; a rustic is jealous of his sweetheart; and a young lover is jealous, not of his mistress, but his money, which he contrives to get out of his guardian’s clutches, by affecting to be deeply in debt, and receiving his supposed creditors’ demands by personating them all, one after another. We cannot travel into the plot more elaborately: there is hardly a joke in the piece, good, bad or indifferent, except its manual wit: when the husband talks about toying another woman, the wife says, "I'll love you," and the husband replies, that he has had enough of her love; and when he adds, that he only kissed the forbidden woman, the wife exclaims, "I'll kiss you," to which the husband replies, that he had rather she should not: excepting these two, or rather this one bon-mot, we recollect none other. Mr. Dowton too was condemned to act in this unhappy Farce: he stormed with passion, and raved with jealousy; but the author had provided him with no adequate motive for either. We never witnessed a piece of so little intention; the moment and the actors were trusted to entirely, and we had rather have had "a play extempore" at once. No effect can be produced without a cause.

Mr. Pocock has hitherto had most of his comic songs written for him; but we should suppose he had slipped his leading-strings in the Green-ey'd Monster, his verse is so ricketty and larmoyant. Mr. Dowton brawled an irregular mad-song about Jealousy; and Mr. Lovegrove toiled through another about the Comet; but it evidently went against him, and when called upon to repeat it, he gave the speaking mimicry, or patter of it (as it is technically called) word for word, and tone for tone, as he had laboured it the first time. We wish him well out of the part, and the piece well off the list; but it was damned the first night, and will therefore "be repeated every evening," &c. &c. The music, by Mr. Welsh, is theatrical, and may pass. With such actors as Dowton and Lovegrove, why do not this Company revive some of Foote's Farces, which they may get for nothing, and not pay Pococks and bawcocks for making fools of them and the town?

On Friday, Mr. H. Lewis, son of the late vivacious comedian of that name, performed the character of the madman Tangent in Mr. Morton's monstrous anomaly called the Way to get Married. This performer made an essay in London a few years ago, and is now we believe regularly engaged here. His line of acting is precisely that of his late father; and if his performances will occasionally remind us with delight of that soul of whim, they will also call from the dead many such disgusting pieces of rottenness as the Way to get Married; so that we are in doubt, whether we shall not suffer more than we shall benefit by the acquisition. The Way to get Married, by a strange and most violent misnomer called a comedy, is an inconsistent compound of vulgarity and sentiment, a low shop-comedy, reflecting the city instead of the court, its wit from 'Change-alley, and its plot from the Rules of the Fleet; in one scene you shall hear of pickles and congou, and in the next of suicide, and imprecations to Heaven to blast with its hottest vengeance; instead of entertaining us with a war of wits, the characters trust to their heels, their cudgels, or the chairs and tables; and when you expect a bon mot, the party drops on his knees, and discovers a great gift in prayer. And yet, with all its sentiment and piety, the play can be indecent enough; but then it is vulgarly and openly so, without the disingenuous and glazing equivoques, with which the licentious wit of our old dramatists is cloaked. In Mr. Morton's play, a young man talks of pandaring for an old one, in plain terms, before the face of the audience, calling every thing by its right name. We must not suffer ourselves to be led farther into this subject, limited as we are at present for space; but we have not witnessed a more disgusting play than the Way to get Married, since the commencement of our attendance at the Theatres.

Mr. Lewis does not so strongly resemble his late father in person, as he does in voice and manner: his complexion is fair, and his hair red, so that he appears in full powder: when he warms, his eyes and teeth discover much of the animation of his father's look. At first we thought he rather laboured, and imitated his archetype externally, than from the soul within. But he improved as he proceeded; and seemed really to have inherited our late favourite's spirit and vivacity. He has the same restlessness, the same flings and rolls of the limbs, the same insinuation of finger and squeak of voice, the same flutter of hand, and the same impatience to slur over the dashes of honest feeling, with which his line of character is occasionally clouded. Mr. Lewis's countenance is too fair to be so expressive as his father's; and he wants the self-abandonment of his parent: he may improve, however, in the confidence which will produce this; and the more closely he resembles his father, the better the town will like him: what would have been servile imitation in another man, will be only lawful inheritance in him. If the comedies of Morton and Reynolds must be revived, Mr. Lewis will certainly be an important enlivener of them; but, for ourselves, we rather think we could forego both the corpses and their resurrection-man, "body and soul together," with much Christian patience and resignation.
The Haymarket Theatre closed on Tuesday night with the following address, spoken by Mr. Elliston:—

p.quote: "I am desired, Ladies and Gentlemen, by the Managers of this Theatre, to inform you, that, on this night, they close a season of experiment, which has been adopted to save their interests from annihilation. Without meaning to advance any complaint against their great rivals,—the superiority of whose theatrical privileges such rivals have, certainly, a right to exercise to their own advantage,—without any intention of this nature, the Managers here beg leave to state, that the increasing protraction of performances in what are called the Winter Houses, and the extensive controul those houses possess over persons engaged by them, have created an imperious necessity of establishing, as nearly as it has yet been found possible, a company of performers independent of other London Playhouses, as the only method of preventing their property from being totally destroyed, before farther means may have been elected to guard it. In such an arduous struggle, through the known generosity of this metropolis, the Managers have met encouragement; if not to that extent which may conduce to their present profit, at least in a proportion to give them hope, that (in addition to their humble solicitation to be relieved from certain restrictions), their perseverance to entertain you, and, from time to time, an accumulation of new talents, will crown their efforts with that ultimate success which British patronage is sure to promote, in consideration of those who assiduously labour to deserve it. This Theatre will re-open at the earliest period granted to its licence. The Performers, Ladies and Gentlemen, beg to join their most respectful thanks to those of the Managers; and we take our leave under those grateful impressions which your liberality must ever indelibly fix upon our bosoms."
